title: Self-Generated Persuasion
description: People believe conclusions far more when they reach them themselves.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: A conclusion you argue for yourself is more convincing than one handed to you. Ask someone to explain why something is true, and they persuade themselves in the process.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Generating an argument requires active thought, produces a memory of having reasoned it out, and avoids the resistance that comes with being told what to think.

sections.title: Real-Life Examples
content: A salesperson asking "what would you use this for?" lets the buyer sell themselves.
A manager asking a team to argue for a plan produces stronger commitment than simply announcing it.

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: Open questions that invite the other person to make the case.
A discussion designed so the target states the conclusion first.

sections.title: Ethical Uses
sections.content: Genuine questioning helps people think clearly and own their decisions.

sections.title: Manipulative Uses
sections.content: Steering someone with narrow questions until they talk themselves into a position you wanted.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: A conversation where every path leads to one predetermined answer.
Being asked to justify something before you have decided.

sections.title: Defense Strategies
content: Slow down before you state a conclusion out loud; you may be building your own case.
Ask what the other options are.

sections.title: Mistakes People Make
content: Underestimating how much your own words shape your beliefs.
Believing you decided freely when you were guided.

sections.title: Key Lessons
content: We are most persuaded by ourselves.
Notice when you are the one making the case.
